subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL  CORRECTION OF NEWSPAPER REPORTS RESPECTING SALE OF URANIUM TO RUSSIA

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL  CORRECTION OF NEWSPAPER REPORTS RESPECTING SALE OF URANIUM TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege pertaining to two articles written by Mr. A. I. Goldberg of Moscow, reproduced in various Canadian newspapers and commented upon fairly extensively. The facts should be recorded.
The first article, printed in the newspapers of April 15, reads as follows:
Trade Minister Churchill said here Thursday that Canada would be willing to sell the Soviet union uranium from Blind River, Ontario, mines. Mr. Churchill, in Moscow to sign a new Russian-Cana-dian trade agreement, said, in reply to questions, that the Russians wanted Canadian uranium.
The second article, printed on April 16, reads in part as follows:
He said there was a "misunderstanding" about a statement he made on his arrival here two days ago that Canada "would sell uranium to the Russians if they want it." This reporter asked, "Would you sell uranium to the Russians under your new trade agreement"? Churchill's reply was, "Yes, if they would want it."
The quotations I have read from the two articles are false in their entirety. The true story of this episode is as follows. Immediately on my arrival on the 14th of April at the National hotel in Moscow I met Mr. Goldberg in the corridor for a period of about 30 seconds. We exchanged greetings. Mr. Goldberg said he had been in the Blind River area a few years ago, and I said I had recently been there on a visit. There was no discussion of the uranium stretch-out program nor any reference to the proposed trade agreement as he writes in his article. He stated that Canada had a surplus of uranium, and I said "Yes".
Then he put to me the following question, and this was his only question: "If Russia wants to buy uranium from Canada are you willing to sell?"
Uranium is not a product to be dealt with lightly. It is used for nuclear bombs. The question was obviously a trap, so I did not answer it. My only comment was, "Canada has plenty of uranium". That was the end of the conversation.
Mr. Goldberg then proceeded to falsify his report and to invent an answer which I did
79951-0-204
not give and to invent a question which he did not ask, namely about the Russians wanting Canadian uranium.
The next meeting with Mr. Goldberg was on Saturday, April 16, at a regular press conference which lasted for almost 40 minutes. In his second dispatch, printed in Canadian papers on April 16, Mr. Goldberg does not mention the press conference nor quote from it, for the simple reason that he took no part in it. He asked no questions, he just sat silently. Uranium was not mentioned by anyone. He had ample opportunity. One of the correspondents asked, "What articles or products does Canada expect to sell to Russia?" I replied, "With the exception of wheat, no particular articles have been mentioned." At that moment Mr. Goldberg might have intervened to challenge my statement. He remained silent.
His report refers to a private meeting that I had with him after the press conference was over. His report of that private meeting reads in part as follows, as printed in the newspapers of April 16:
Today Churchill said: "There was a misunderstanding. I am not here to sell any specific item and selling uranium to the Russians would be the last thing we would do."
The quotation I have just read from Mr. Goldberg's second article is false. Mr. Goldberg appears to have a very unreliable memory. The facts I will now give, based on notes I made of the conversation, for I knew that I would not be able to rely on the veracity of Mr. Goldberg. I had hoped that he would correct his first dispatch, and that was why I saw him privately. It was a vain hope. Instead of correcting his first false story he repeated it and embellished it.
I said to Mr. Goldberg that he obviously misunderstood the problems connected with uranium, for he was writing fantastic nonsense. To test his knowledge of the subject I asked him various questions with regard to uranium being on the list of strategic materials, about the necessity for bilateral agreements before it may be sold even for peaceful purposes, and about the supervision and control of uranium sales. His answers showed that he was well aware of all those matters.
I then said to him that the statement he had attributed to me in his Thursday dispatch was untrue and incomprehensible in

Question of Privilege
view of the knowledge that he had of the restrictions placed on the sale of uranium. Then I added, "The last product that Canada would be willing to sell to Russia at this time is uranium". He said, "I will report that".
He twisted and distorted it. He twisted it to read that the last country to which we would sell uranium would be Russia.
Another paragraph of Mr. Goldberg's report of our private meeting, printed on April 16, reads as follows:
Reminded of his Thursday statement and the context in which he made it, Churchill said, "Well, it was made in a joking way".
The Thursday statement has been given in three versions by Mr. Goldberg who is nothing if not versatile.
The first version was printed on April 15:
Canada would be willing to sell the Soviet union uranium from Blind River, Ontario, mines and the Russians want Canadian uranium.
The second revised version was printed on April 16:
Canada would sell uranium to the Russians if they want it
The third revised version of the same date:
Yes, if they would want it.
I said none of those words at any time. My Thursday statement was simply, "Canada has plenty of uranium".
Goldberg attributes to me a statement that I did not make. Then he writes that he reminded me of that statement and that I said it was made in a joking way.
As I did not make the statement in the first place, in any of the three versions, Mr. Goldberg is obviously falsifying the record again.
There was never any joking on my part about uranium nor any statement by me that I had been joking.
I asked Mr. Goldberg what purpose he had in mind in inquiring about the sale of uranium to Russia. He would not answer that question. I then accused him of making a farce and a joke of a serious matter with a careless disregard for the consequences. No responsible person, knowing that uranium is the material that is used for nuclear bombs, would talk lightly, in this period of international tension, about selling it to any country as if it were just another commodity.
So that there may be no mistake about it,
I would add that at no time during the course of the lengthy negotiations with the Russians either here in Canada or in Moscow was the subject of uranium mentioned by any one of the officials or the ministers on either side.

In conclusion may I express my surprise that in the midst of the turmoil that appears to have upset some editorial offices in Canada no contact was made with me. No representative of the press of Canada at home or abroad, no representative of any other news-gathering service, got in touch with me. There were no interviews, there were no cablegrams, there were no telephone calls.
It is regrettable that Mr. Goldberg's dispatches, on the vitally important subject of uranium, at a critical moment in the trade negotiations with Russia, were accepted in Canada without any attempt whatsoever at verification.

subtopic: VISIT OF GENERAL DE GAULLE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VISIT OF GENERAL DE GAULLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of certain events which took place during the Easter recess perhaps the house will allow me to make a statement, first on the visit of President de Gaulle and second on a return visit which I paid to Mexico.
The recent state visit of the President of the French republic and community, General de Gaulle, provided the Canadian government and people with an opportunity to pay tribute to one of the foremost statesmen of our time, the illustrious leader of one of Canada's

mother countries. Together with my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and members of the cabinet, a most satisfactory exchange of views took place during the stay of the president in Ottawa. The international situation was discussed, as well as the question of disarmament, aid to underdeveloped countries and other subjects of equal mutual interest.
These exchanges of views served to emphasize the continuing need for full consultation among members of NATO on matters which affect the vital interests of the western world. Coming as it did just two weeks before the summit conference, an excellent opportunity was presented to make known to him the views of the Canadian government on the major subjects which will be discussed at the conference.
I will not go into detail with regard to those discussions except to say that they covered the range of those matters which are of peculiar and particular interest at this time. I need hardly add that relations between our two countries continue to be excellent, and a wide measure of agreement exists on current world issues.
Following the course of the past, and with the consent of the house, I move that the address which President de Gaulle delivered at the state luncheon on April 19, 1960 and the address delivered by the Prime Minister be included as an appendix to the official report of debates for the third session of this parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: VISIT OF GENERAL DE GAULLE
speechtext:
May I say that we agree with great pleasure to the inclusion of these addresses in Hansard. They will be a memento of a happy visit to our country of a great and towering figure of our times, a man who never lost faith, during what appeared to be defeat, either in the cause for which his country was fighting or in the destiny of that country which in a very special way is our country, too. It will be a memento also of a man who once again has been called to the service of his native land and to the service of peace in difficult times, and who once again has responded to that call with courage and devotion.
I am sure the President's visit to Ottawa and to other parts of Canada will serve to strengthen the bonds which are already so strong between our two countries.

subtopic: VISIT OF GENERAL DE GAULLE
speechtext:
The visit of President de Gaulle to Canada was most welcome to our nation, and emphasized once again the very close relations between Canada and France.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO MEXICO

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO MEXICO
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, I returned the visit paid to Canada last October by President Lopez Mateos, the first Mexican head of state to be an official guest of this country. I did this during the Easter recess.
If the regard and esteem of a people for another can be gauged by the welcome given to their official representatives, the three days I spent in Mexico have brought home to me, more vividly than anything I had ever heard or read, a realization of the good will that Canada enjoys in this dynamic and rapidly advancing North American neighbour.
During this visit I had occasion to discuss with the President and with the foreign minister, Sr. Manuel Tello, questions of concern to both our countries, including international questions, and as a result of these conversations I can say there are no basic differences in our approach to world problems although our policies may not always coincide; and do not, with regard to the law of the sea, where the need to maintain historical rights confirmed by treaty makes it impossible, in the President's view, for Mexico to support the Canadian stand.
These conversations have further convinced me of the need for consultations at a high level with the political leaders not only of countries associated with Canada by tradition and alliance, but those of all other states

Visit to Mexico by Prime Minister whose similarities in background, outlook and interests are bringing them closer to us, in order to reach a wider and clearer understanding of the motives and requirements on which our respective attitudes are based, and to explore the possibilities of more effective collaboration.
I was glad to hear the views of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) a moment ago when he paid his tribute to the need for these exchanges. I can say one thing, that my visit to the various commonwealth countries was worth while in that it provided me with a knowledge and understanding of the attitudes of the other members of the commonwealth which could not have been attained in any other way.
On behalf of the people of Canada I made a presentation to the national university of Mexico of volumes relating to various aspects of Canadian life and achievement.
I could speak of the welcome I was accorded in many ways. As a lawyer I naturally was deeply touched by the fact that for the first time in its history a foreigner was made an honorary member of the illustrious and national college of advocates, a tribute by the bar of Mexico not to me personally but to the people of Canada.
There was a wide measure of public sympathy with the attitude of the Canadian government on matters such as disarmament and the suspension of nuclear tests, to which the hon. member for Assiniboia just referred, the need for international co-operation in the use and development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes, a reduction of discriminatory trade restrictions, the value of fostering cultural relations and an increase in the exchange of students through the granting of scholarships and other facilities.
May I summarize this. I think visits such as this contribute to good will, good fellowship and better understanding. There are no words I can use to describe the warmth of the feeling of the President, the government and the people of Mexico to Canada. I hope the President may be able again very soon to pay a visit to Canada so that we in turn may continue in that close feeling and warm relationship that prevails between our two countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of lhe Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house, and certainly we on this side, were pleased when we learned that the Prime Minister was able to take time off from what might have been a vacation to return the visit of the President of Mexico. I am sure also that this visit has


made its own contribution to the strengthening of the political, cultural and trade relations between two countries which over the years have built up a tradition of friendly relationships. After all, Mr. Speaker, there is a special bond between Mexico and Canada because, with the oceans, we surround the United States.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT TO MEXICO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. believes that a visit such as the Prime Minister has made to Mexico is of a kind that is likely to lead to a strengthening of the relationships between our two countries. We would hope it would lead to an expansion of trade, and be viewed as an indication of Canada's growing interest in the development of good will between Canada and the Latin-American nations and an indication of our concern for their improved economic development.
The Prime Minister made brief reference to some words I used earlier. I want to tell him we feel that exchanges between Canada and other nations should be undertaken from time to time. We say that when these visits are considered the Prime Minister should have in mind their timing and duration, because the Prime Minister's attention to domestic matters as well as external matters is of great importance. We feel that the visit to Mexico was one that probably should have been made.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: TABLING OF PROTOCOL AND LETTERS RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I now table for the information of the house the text of the protocol signed in Moscow on April 18, 1960, which renews for a three-year period the trade agreement between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics of February 29, 1956, as well as the understanding set out in the letters which the two parties exchanged at that time concerning the right of the Canadian government to fix under the Canadian Customs Act values of goods for ordinary and special duty.
The protocol also provides that each of the two governments will give sympathetic consideration to any representations which the other government may make concerning the implementation of the renewed agreement and with regard to other matters which may affect their commercial relations. The protocol is in force provisionally from the date of signature. It is to be ratified as soon as possible, and will enter into force definitively on the date of exchange of instruments of ratification, which is to take place

in Ottawa. An early opportunity will be provided for a debate in parliament, and a resolution of approval will be introduced to this end.
I am also tabling copies of letters which I exchanged with the Soviet minister of foreign trade, Mr. N. S. Patolichev, setting forth certain additional understandings concerning the development of trade between the two countries. If the house agrees, I suggest that the text of the protocol and of the letters be printed as an appendix to Votes and Proceedings.

subtopic: TABLING OF PROTOCOL AND LETTERS RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH RUSSIA
speechtext:
As hon. members are aware, the negotiations for renewal of the trade agreement with the U.S.S.R. took a considerable time. They were initiated before the 1956 agreement lapsed on February 28, 1959, and the early discussions were not without difficulties. However, common ground was eventually found, and the agreement is being renewed on terms which I consider satisfactory from the Canadian point of view, particularly taking into account the changed trading circumstances since the earlier agreement was concluded.
The house is familiar with the provisions of the 1956 agreement which is now being extended. In brief, Canada and the U.S.S.R. exchange most favoured nation treatment and, on a reciprocal basis, provide for nondiscriminatory treatment of merchant ships in the seaports of the two countries. Either government may, however, apply prohibitions or restrictions of any kind directed to the protection of its essential security interests. Our strategic export controls are therefore not affected.
The protocol extending the agreement broadens the basis on which representations can be addressed to either of the two parties. Previously the two governments had agreed to give sympathetic consideration to representations concerning the implementation of the agreement. The scope for such representations has now been enlarged to include any other matters affecting commercial relations between the two countries. Should the necessity arise this would permit Canada, for example, to take up with the government of the U.S.S.R. any special problems which may
25. 1960
Trade Agreement with Russia be encountered in respect of the sale in world markets of Soviet products in which Canada has a substantial export interest.
The letter which I exchanged with Mr. Patolichev provides that in each year of the renewed agreement the Soviet foreign trade organizations will purchase Canadian goods up to a total value of $25 million Canadian, including not less than 200,000 metric tons of Canadian wheat, provided the total annual value of Canadian purchases from the U.S.S.R. is not less than $12J million Canadian. Should the total value of Canadian purchases from the U.S.S.R. be less than $12J million Canadian in any one year the Soviet undertaking to purchase from Canada would be reduced and would be determined on a two to one basis; that is, the Soviet union would purchase twice as much from Canada as Canada imported from the Soviet union, and wheat will constitute not less than half the value of such annual Soviet purchases.
It will be noted that no commitment to purchase Soviet goods has been made by the Canadian government. As in the case of trade with other countries, the level of our purchases will be determined by the commercial decisions of Canadian importers. The house will appreciate that the U.S.S.R. agreement to trade with Canada on a two to one basis represents a very substantial concession on their part, since the Soviet union normally endeavours to balance trade with each of its trading partners.
In addition to establishing the Soviet commitment to purchase Canadian goods the letter provides that the authorities of the two countries will meet at least once a year, alternately in Ottawa and Moscow, to consult concerning the implementation of the agreement and any other matters affecting Soviet-Canadian trade relations. It is the hope of both parties that trade will flow reasonably regularly in each year of this agreement. The annual consultations will provide the occasion for an exchange of views with respect to the operation of the agreement. They should also prove of value in building up greater understanding between the two countries with respect to trade matters.
The letter also sets forth an understanding that as a measure toward attaining the mutual objective of an expansion of trade the two governments will facilitate visits for business purposes between the two countries. It is my hope that within the framework of the renewed agreement, and in pursuance of the undertakings in the letter which has been exchanged, there will be a mutually advantageous growth in trade between the two countries. The actual growth in trade and the nature of the goods to be exchanged

Trade Agreement with Russia will depend mainly on the decisions of the businessmen and business organizations of the two countries.
The Canadian market is highly competitive, and it will be necessary for the Soviet export authorities to understand our requirements if they are to sell successfully in Canada. Similarly, it will be important for Canadian exporters to make known to the Soviet import organizations the products and goods which they are in a position to supply on competitive terms. In general, it will be necessary for there to be much closer contact between the traders of the two countries than has been the case in the past. To this end I have suggested, and the Soviet authorities have agreed, that a group of Soviet traders representing both export and import interests should visit Canada, and the Soviet authorities have indicated that they would welcome a comparable visit of Canadian businessmen to the Soviet union. I hope the necessary arrangements for these visits can be made during the current year. I have also invited the Soviet minister of trade, Mr. Patolichev, to come to Canada and this invitation is being considered by the Soviet government. I hope he will find it convenient to come at the same time as the visit of Soviet trade representatives.
As a further measure to facilitate the growth of trade, Mr. W. J. Van Vliet has been appointed commercial counsellor at the Canadian embassy in Moscow, where his main responsibility will be to assist in the promotion of our exports to the U.S.S.R.
The house will recall that under the 1956 arrangement the Soviet union undertook an annual obligation to purchase a specified minimum quantity of wheat, 400,000 tons. The new arrangement provides that at least half the value of the annual Soviet purchase commitment will be in the form of wheat. If Soviet purchases were to rise to the value of $25 million, our sales would include at least 200,000 tons of wheat. Accordingly, while the Soviet union will continue to purchase significant quantities of Canadian wheat, we may now look toward more diversified sales to the U.S.S.R. Both sides are aiming to diversify as well as to expand trade.
The house is aware that the Soviet union has greatly enlarged its production of wheat and is a regular wheat exporter. In the circumstances the amount of wheat which the Soviet union has undertaken to purchase may be regarded as satisfactory. I should add that I raised with the Soviet government the question of the approximately 200,000 tons of wheat still outstanding under the old agreement. Provided trade develops in a satisfactory manner, in accordance with the agreement and

the letters exchanged in Moscow, I was assured by Mr. Patolichev that the Soviet union would endeavour to make up this deficiency so there would be no question of the Soviet union not having fulfilled the earlier obligation.
I should like the house to know, Mr. Speaker, that I was received with friendship and courtesy by the Soviet ministers and senior officials whom I had the opportunity to meet. In addition to Mr. Patolichev I had the pleasure of general discussions with Mr. F. R. Kozlov and Mr. A. I. Mikoyan, both first deputy premiers of the Soviet union. These gentlemen showed a welcome awareness of Canada's interests as a world trader and major exporter.
Our conversations were frank and constructive. The hospitality which was shown to me and to the other members of the Canadian delegation was generous and memorable. I believe that over and above the provisions of the agreement and the exchange of letters, a basis has been established for closer and more fruitful co-operation between the two countries in the field of trade.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the minister is somewhat longer than is usual on motions, and in addition to giving the factual information which we all welcome and which is properly given at this stage of the house proceedings on a subject of this importance, it also contains some debatable material. In so far as it contained factual information and related to the tabling of the documents relevant to the new trade treaty, we welcome it because this will give us an opportunity of examining the actual documentation to see precisely what the situation is. We welcome also the announcement that in due course the matter will be coming before the house for discussion.
The minister described the agreement, if I understood him correctly, as satisfactory in the circumstances. His later elaboration of it would lead us to believe it is not necessarily so satisfactory, because it does not even provide for the taking up of the requirements for wheat provided under the earlier agreement, although it is quite true that they may take that additional 200,000 tons and thus complete the earlier agreement. While he told us how high the obligation to purchase might go if our Canadian importers bought heavily from Russia, he did not tell us what I took from his statement to be a fact, that it could also go much lower than it has been if our importers do not buy.
I noted also the omission to deal with the list of prohibited goods for export to Russia.

Perhaps when we come to orders of the day we can get some further information on that point. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, there is no purpose in making further comment at this time.

subtopic: TABLING OF PROTOCOL AND LETTERS RESPECTING AGREEMENT WITH RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our group was very happy to learn that the minister was in Moscow, and that at long last he was able to complete the renewal of our trade agreement with the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. We note with considerable interest that, unless I am in error, this is the first time the Canadian government has entered into what is in effect a reciprocal trade agreement, in that we agree to buy a certain amount of goods from another nation if another nation will buy a certain quantity of goods from us.
It is our hope that our government will realize its responsibility in this regard. We regret very much that even if the optimistic objectives that are aimed at under the agreement are realized, it will involve a reduction in Russia's purchase of Canadian wheat under the earlier agreement by 50 per cent. We regret very much this proposed reduction in Russia's purchase of Canadian wheat.
However, we want to emphasize, and to underline as heavily as we can, that for the first time to our knowledge, in signing a trade agreement, the Canadian government has morally, if not otherwise, accepted a responsibility. I noted the minister's announcement that a counsellor had been appointed to serve in Moscow to promote Canadian exports. I hope the government will realize that under the terms of the agreement, exports will automatically follow our imports. I hope the minister might see fit to exert considerable energy toward the promotion of Canadian imports from the Soviet union, and that those efforts might extend beyond the expression of pious pleas and platitudes to Canadian enterprise to actively consider the importation of goods made within the Soviet union, because our exports are so directly related to Canadian imports under the terms of the agreement. We hope the government will realize its responsibility in this regard and will not be entirely dependent upon the whims of Canadian importers.

Mr. Chairman, the applicant before parliament is a 30-year old private secretary supporting one child on an income of around $250 a month. My purpose in rising is not to bring these humane facts for the consideration of the committee, because I realize that it is of little use or purpose in considering the mischievous animus that activates a few people who have acted in this way for some time.
I was glad my hon. friend from Skeena did not bring up the point that there had been any lobbying in connection with this case because it might have had a very serious effect

Private Bills-Divorce on whether or not this bill should properly go through parliament. The respondent's husband has been referred to as a member of the Royal Canadian Air Force. A few days ago he flew to Egypt. Before he went he had been in touch with me several times. He had arranged for a marriage again and quite a considerable sum of money had been spent. He asked whether it would not be possible for the C.C.F. to change its filibuster tactics and allow his bill to go through so that his money would not have been spent in vain. I told him of the rule against lobbying which I had propounded here on previous occasions, and told him definitely to stay away from the House of Commons, not to approach any members and to take his financial licking. Perhaps some day, not at this session but some other time, there would not be this mischievous behaviour on the part of a certain few denying the minority their rights. I gather he has done that and has left the country, poorer for having contracted a marriage and paid a large sum of money and not having been able to go through with it.

I should not say this is precisely new, but in one sense it is new. I had understood, not from the hon. member for Halifax directly but from someone else, that there was one particular case in this group with which we are now dealing, in which some marriage arrangement had been concluded based upon the hope that the petition would be granted. I did not know that this was the particular case. I knew nothing about it, or whether there had been any lobbying or importuning of members to hurry up or slow down or anything of that nature.
I would have liked to make some comments about the very things the hon. member for Halifax mentioned. As you know, it is my contention that in those cases where children are concerned we should give a greater degree of consideration to them. I refrained from doing that because the hon. member for Halifax raised a point of order on a previous occasion when I dealt with the question of children. You, yourself, sir, were in the chair at that time and ruled that we had no jurisdiction with respect to children or their maintenance. Your colleague, who is in the chair occasionally in your absence, also made a similar ruling. As a matter of fact, I think he made the same ruling with respect to me four or five times.
The reason I refrained from mentioning the fact that there were children, except to point out that there was one child which indicated the consummation of the marriage, was this ruling. However, there is reference to the income of the petitioner, the fact she looks after the child and that she is working.


All this information is in here. I am very pleased that the hon. member for Halifax did mention this subject. As I say, I did not because I did not want to run afoul of your ruling, even though I know that each member of the committee is vitally concerned about the welfare of the children in any one of these cases. By the ruling, however, we are forbidden to concern ourselves with that. I would say that on each occasion in which there are children concerned I will do the best I can to go as far as I can in the direction of wondering orally about the welfare of the children.
In this particular case, the petitioner has been given the legal custody of the child by the court. As the hon. member for Halifax indicated, the mother is a private secretary with an income of about $280 per month. The child is four, probably a little over four by now, and is looked after by an aunt while the mother is at work. The mother sees the child every night, and sees that he is properly looked after. If these circumstances persist it does appear that the child will get along fairly well in so far as material maintenance is concerned. If the woman marries again, there will be a father and mother for the child. The husband came to see the child very seldom.
As I say, I do not want to go too far in that direction and cause you, Mr. Chairman, too much exercise in getting up and down to call me to order, even though I know this is something that is in the minds of other members of the committee and even though they may vote against particular motions we might move at some time in order to ask permission to discuss the children themselves.
From the remarks of the hon. member for Halifax I took a certain inference. He made some reference to the mischievous few and said that because of the actions of that mischievous few some people were not having their petitions for divorce dealt with as expeditiously as they might have expected, having regard to the procedure in years past. From what the hon. member for Halifax said I also assume that he is referring to me as being one of the mischievous few and to the hon. member for Timiskaming as being the other half of the mischievous few. Whether or not this is so, he did not say, but I think I am entitled to take that attitude.
Seriously, may I say this? While the hon. member for Halifax may allege that this action is mischievousness,-a description which would indicate that it is not sincere-I think I should be afforded the opportunity of making a comment in rebuttal thereto in order to point out to the hon. member for Halifax that such is not the case. It is not a question of mischievousness. It is not a

question of lack of care or concern for the individuals involved but rather of the greatest appreciation for the domestic problems they have and of great sorrow-in some cases more than in others, depending on the circumstances, of course-for the steps that these people are obliged to take in order to obtain relief from their marital problems. They are steps which are not available to people living in other provinces; they necessitate long delays, in many cases up to a year.
In this particular case, I find from a quick look, it is almost one year ago-May 13, 1959 -that the adultery took place. In any event, even if we had not debated and discussed these particular divorce bills to the extent that we are discussing them, with the particular goal we have in mind, it would have been 10 or 11 months anyway before the petitioner here could have had any hope of getting a divorce granted or of getting relief from her problems. In some cases the time range is over a year.
This situation arises because this particular petitioner here and others must take the step of petitioning parliament, that parliament can deal with these petitions for divorce only when it is in session and that it is not in session all the year round. We set up rules governing the procedure. The other place does so and we do so by our standing orders. We set up rules with regard to private bills. These rules say that you must have your application in by a certain time. If you do not have it in by a certain time, parliament is not going to deal with it anyway. A person might find himself or herself just over that borderline of the time limit and having to wait until the next session. It is a question of costs which range in amount, on the average, to twice as much as they do in any other province. For these things we have great concern.
There are also other matters but these are vitally important ones. There is the question of the welfare and maintenance of children, a matter with which we have no right to concern ourselves or to deal with. We can grant a divorce but we cannot take any action to deal with the children themselves. This is another unfortunate thing. This jurisdiction should be vested in the same place so that-

To the extent that the courts under those laws are able to deal with the maintenance of children, yes, possibly that is so. We think there are alternatives to this particular matter which would be much fairer than the situation is at the present moment. We think there are alternatives to the present system of parliament having to deal with these matters.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the point raised by the hon. member for Halifax I would like to point out that while it is true we are concerned with each individual as he or she comes before us-and we appreciate the fact that the chairman of the committee has advised against lobbying as in years gone by-it still should be borne in mind that we weigh each of these cases on its merits, not on granting the divorce. It may be quite fortunate that in this particular case the divorce has not been granted previously, particularly when this gentleman is being transferred to Egypt, as I understand it. If he had not remarried by the time he left here, if he had obtained this divorce it is possible he would have been married in Egypt and his problem might have been international rather than just of a local nature.
In this particular case there was an alimony settlement made in the province of Quebec which awarded the wife $100 a month, and she drew that for a little over two years, amounting in all to about $2,400. If he had not paid this alimony or been in a position where he had to pay it, then he would have been able to pay $2,500 for the divorce and there would have been no problem.
As it is, if the chairman of the miscellaneous private bills committee checks up he will find he has been able to save $100 a month from September to May because the wife decided she did not want the $100. So there is that amount of money available as a down payment for this divorce in any event.
I do not think that any consideration should be given to the argument that delay is taking place. I think we should be ashamed of ourselves for what has gone on in the past rather than attach any blame to anyone for going into these particular cases. In this case we are concerned with a point made by the hon. member for Skeena, that the maintenance for the child has been discussed in a particular case, and we will find it in the 48th report. I would like to quote what the lawyer said because at that time he was referring to this matter. On page 12 senator Farquhar asked:
Q. If you get this divorce is he bound to continue paying that $75?
That is the amount awarded in the civil court in Quebec. Then Mr. Usher said:
Senator, probably I would be better able to answer that question. Under our jurisprudence, once there is a divorce the obligation to support the wife ceases, but the obligation to support the child remains. If there is a judgment rendered by the

superior court of Montreal awarding alimony in favour of children a divorce in Ottawa does not affect that, because it is not an alimentary payment to the wife. Mr. Justice Mackinnon, I think it was, in around the year 1952 or 1953 rendered a judgment to that effect, that a divorce does not affect the alimony payable for children.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that statement, if it is factual-and I have no reason to think it is not-has and should have a bearing on what we do in relationship to payments to the wife and children, and particularly the desire we have expressed many times that the superior court in the province of Quebec should make these decisions rather than leave them to us in Ottawa when we have not the jurisdiction to make those particular rulings.
This case is an interesting case, as the hon. member for Skeena pointed out. There are a number of facts in this case which we have not been concerned with in other cases, and I think for that reason we should give some consideration to the problems arising from this source. I would like to read a short part of the evidence appearing on page 12 of the 47th report, as follows:
Q. But when did you stop living together as man and wife?
A. In the summer of 1957.
Q. What sort of life did you have with your husband for a year or two prior to the summer of 1957?
A. Very bad.
Q. What was the trouble?
A. He was not home very often and I saw a social worker.
To digress, I would suggest that very few people employed in the air force, particularly in certain fields, are home, and this does not always warn of bad relations unless other factors are hinted at which are not discussed at all in this case, and that is the complaint of mental cruelty. The report goes on:
Q. When did you see a social worker?
A. In the summer of 1957.
Q. Why did you see a social worker?
A. Because I was feeling kind of sick.
Q. Did you consult a doctor?
A. Oh, yes. I did.
Q. What did you learn?
A. I learned that he had given me a venereal disease.
Q. Did you take treatment?
A. Yes.
Q. Are you all right now?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you have venereal disease at the time of your marriage?
A. No, sir.
Q. From the time you learned about that- it was in the summer of 1957 that you learned about that?
A. Yes.
Q. -up to the present time have you lived with your husband as man and wife?
A. No, sir.
Mr. Chairman, this raises in my opinion, a number of questions. One of them is the
Private Bills-Divorce
question that some consideration should be given to these people in a social service way which would eliminate probably some of the disagreement which appears to have arisen from the employment of this particular airman and the fact that he had to be away from home for some time. I was interested to know what the effect would be in relation to this venereal disease charge, because I understand this is a factor in separation and divorce proceedings and has a connection with what the courts decide in these particular cases. On page 337 of Kent Power's authoritative work on jurisprudence in Canada appears the following:
Proof that the defendant husband is suffering from a venereal disease may be accepted, according to the circumstances, as sufficient evidence of adultery unless the contracting of the disease is satisfactorily explained.
Then reference is made to an Alberta case,
L.	v L., where the defendant husband was shown to be suffering from syphilis.
It was of recent origin and there was complete absence of evidence other than the testimony of the defendant to indicate that he might have been affected innocently. The court accepted as true the testimony of the plaintiff that she had not had sexual intercourse with any man other than the defendant. He also testified that he had not committed adultery with any person since his marriage to the plaintiff nearly five years previously. It was held that this statement of his was not of sufficient evidence in the circumstances to repudiate the presumption arising from the other evidence that he had committed adultery. Therefore an order nisi should be granted.
Reference is made to a number of other cases of that nature, and it is pointed out that in each of these cases sufficient evidence of this kind will constitute reason for a separation on the ground of mental cruelty. It is further pointed out on page 537 that where the communication of venereal disease is relied on as constituting cruelty it is not necessary to plead or prove that it was communicated wilfully, negligently or recklessly. Reference is made to the case of Browning v. Browning in 1911, where it was stated that in practice, unless a defendant is able to prove that he obtained venereal disease in a manner that would be acceptable to the courts, transmission of the disease is sufficient to constitute evidence of adultery.
This being an acceptable method of establishing adultery, I am surprised that the committee of the other place and the lawyer handling this case did not place more emphasis upon this aspect of the petition. It must certainly have led to medical attention being given at the time. If the facts are as stated it could probably be proved that this disease was communicated without any care being taken as to the results. If this is an acceptable method of establishing adultery

Private Bills-Divorce
charges-and the leading authority in Canada appears to accept it as such-I am surprised that a counsel with the experience of Mr. Lieff would go to the trouble of bringing in evidence of adultery at a later date. The court in the province of Quebec must already have given consideration to this matter; it awarded alimony and a separation on that basis.
To return to the evidence, the question is asked: Was there any agreement? The answer is given in the negative. Then questions were asked about reconciliation, as follows:
Q. Was there any chance of reconciliation between yourself and your husband?
A. No.
Q. Did you do all you could to make a success of this matter?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you give your husband any reason for running around with anybody else?
A. No, sir.
Q. While you were with him did you consult a psychiatrist about his behaviour?
A. Yes.
Q. Did you tell the psychiatrist your problems?
A. Yes.
Q. And about your husband's?
A. Yes.
I am surprised that the chairman of the Senate committee should have allowed these questions to be asked without seeking to arrive at the reason why the psychiatrist was consulted and what the result of the treatment was; whether the wife was to be treated for some quirk of a mental nature, or whether the husband was suffering from some such affliction. I am sure that if the Minister of National Defence were here he would immediately say that an airman would obviously not be so affected and that therefore it would be the woman who was bene-fitting from psychiatric treatment, because, certainly, air force personnel are not suffering in this way or they would be in a mental hospital or receiving treatment from another source.
I should like, now, to consider the evidence as given by Mr. Steele. I am particularly interested in knowing how they found out who this man was. There was a reference to the fact that they knew which hotel room they were in, No. 944-
It is quite all right. The hon. member can leave. I think there is a quorum.
The evidence at this point reads:
By Mr. Lieff:
Q. Mr. Steele, can you identify the photograph which has been filed as Exhibit No. 2?
A. Yes, it is Joseph Hould.
Q. Did you investigate his behaviour?
A. Yes, I did.
Q. When?
A. I first started the investigation in February, 1959, but nothing really happened until May, 1959. He is with the air force and he would be flying in and out every other day of the week. On May 11

I had information that he was in town and I checked at the air base and found that he was in some hotel in Montreal. From investigation at the hotels I found that he was in the Laurentian hotel. Investigation showed that he had been in there on the 11th but I did not see him until the 12th. There was a Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Hould registered in the Laurentian hotel, room 944. In the evening I called Roy Humphries to join me at the hotel, which he did about 7 o'clock. At that time I was in the restaurant, and so were the subjects. When they came out Roy followed them upstairs.
Q. After he came back what did you both do?
A. We both sat around the lobby and they came down in the elevator around 10 o'clock, Mr. Hould and the woman who was with him. They went back about an hour later from the cocktail lounge. Roy followed them up again. We kept observation on that room until 1.30 a.m., which was then May 13. When I gained admittance to the room, after Mr. Hould opened the door, I showed him my identification card and also his photograph and asked him his name and he told me it was Joseph Hould. And then I told him the purpose of our visit.
I call attention to the fact that they do not indicate how they found out where he was. The witness does not say he consulted the register. I am not aware whether a detective has a right to direct a hotel to produce the register or not. If he has, then I am surprised that the witness had not seen the handwriting of this man, or had not looked at the register. On page 14, the witness says:
Q. Did you see the registration?
A. I did
Q. You were not able to check the handwriting?
A. He did not leave it there very long.
I do not know to whom reference is made, but the Laurentian hotel must be a good one to stay away from if the hotel permits private dicks to wander around at will, make entry into rooms at will and conduct an examination of the registry, however briefly, at will. I was previously under the impression that the hotel had a good reputation. I did not know it catered to the divorce mill making its facilities available to detectives in cases of this nature. Perhaps the investigator represented himself as a detective in the employ of the hotel.
Canadians must be damn fools if when they are awakened in the middle of the night by an unknown joker they throw open their doors and welcome him with open arms. I could understand this happening in the bush where you may find a sign on a door inviting you to lift the latch and enter because you will be welcome at any time but this is not true of large cosmopolitan cities. It has not been my experience that you are admitted into homes at three or four in the morning.
Let me cite a personal illustration. In the town of New Liskeard my son recently rented the Legion hall for a teen town dance. After the dance it was discovered that the key to the hall had been taken home by another

executive member. My son went to the homes of three members at a late hour in an attempt to recover the key but no one responded to his knocking at the door. He went to two or three other places but met with no success. Finally I had to get the telephone operator to ring for a long time the telephone of someone I knew before I could get an answer. It simply is not reasonable to ask us to believe that Canadians are so stupid as to welcome strangers at three or four in the morning wearing only shorts or a bath towel. There must be connivance, assistance from the hotel or misrepresentation on the part of the detectives. The detectives give the most flimsy, unsupported and incredible evidence and the chairman who handles these matters has the audacity to say that these bills are being held up unreasonably.
I wish now to deal with another important matter, the posiion of the corespondent in these cases. I have not asked what his position is but if I were a corespondent I believe I would fight the case because my reputation and good name would be at stake. If I did not defend the case it would mean one of two things, that the facts were as stated or that I was hired to do a certain job. It is not for me to decide whether this is connected with the divorce court or the morality set-up in Montreal but some consideration should be given to the corespondent.
In the present case there is some difference of opinion about the address of the corespondent. Mr. Steele in his evidence said that her address was Shawinigan Falls. I do not know where Shawinigan Falls is but I have heard of it and I am sure that a letter addressed there would reach the person for whom it was intended. Reference was made to a Blue Cross card on which the young lady's name was given as Lorna Challow, and her address as Shawinigan Falls. The chairman then asked where the lady was served and the clerk of the committee said she was served at 4132 Parthenais street in the city of Montreal.
What kind of clerk do we have in the Senate? Why would he send notice to her at an address in Montreal when on the basis of the evidence her last known address was Shawinigan Falls? There is no previous reference to the Montreal address. I have served summonses for witnesses and have always understood they should be served in person at the last known address of the individual. It is a serious matter if the corespondent in this case has not been served and does not know she has the opportunity to appear before the Senate and the House of Commons to defend herself.
Private Bills-Divorce
We are certainly not interested in pressing any charges that could be laid as a result of her actions if she admitted them. On the other hand she may not have been served and she may be unaware she has the opportunity to deny the allegations. We have the obligation to ascertain if she ever received notice. Because her last known address is Shawinigan Falls we have no right to assume that notice would have been served at the Montreal address.
This is a serious matter. We are making charges in this case against a third party. In my opinion the third party in these divorce cases should be given the benefit of the doubt even if nobody else is. If this young lady wishes to give evidence to indicate that she is not guilty of adultery and had no part in it I think she should be allowed to do so. Everyone here is aware that there have been discrepancies in cases we have dealt with before. The hon. member for Halifax referred to one that he asked to have referred back. We know of cases where the evidence has not been true, where the respondent was not notified and did not know anything about the proceeding. We know that these cases exist.
We have been asked to deal with one and I suggest that we give the chairman of the committee handling these cases the opportunity to ask for unanimous approval to have this case referred back so that this matter may be cleared up. I should like to ask the sponsor of the bill if he will not agree that this is a matter of grave concern and that the third party may be an innocent party. We know that there are overzealous lawyers and over-zealous detectives. In fact, in many cases the senators may be overzealous because they are under great pressure when they have 500 cases to deal with. They also want to take a holiday of a month so they are under some pressure also. This pressure may be to the detriment of the corespondent in some of these cases. Would it not be in the interests of common decency and justice to refer this case back so that the corespondent's wishes can be ascertained?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that course is necessary in this case. Admittedly there should be an investigation of the methods of service. We are going to have the opportunity to do that in another case, but to proceed merely on the ground of suspicion seems to me a very poor judicial course indeed.

in court to give evidence about something which each of them saw separately and which they were not supposed to work together on. This is evidence of two people working together as a team. I am not as familiar with these documents as I am with the other ones but we shall be after a while.
You are taking a correspondence course.

In another one we shall know where to find this. It is quite simply the notice of the petition that they give to the corespondent. It does not indicate that they have the right to come before the committee and present their side of the case if they feel they have been wrongly accused.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, because of the practice in English law whereby a respondent or corespondent is given the opportunity of disproving the charges that are made against him or her, they should be given notice that they have the opportunity of appearing on this particular day in person.
