The house in committee on Bill No. SD-39, for the relief of Stella Jean Margaret Newman Lamartine-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

I should like to make a few comments about this particular bill before us, and relate them somewhat in the same way as I have the others, to the facts set forth in the bill itself, the marriage and adultery, and whether or not those facts have been proven. In doing so I should like to make reference to the petition itself which indicates in its first paragraph that a lawful marriage did not take place on March 8, 1928, and in the sixth paragraph that on May 25, 1959, at a particular address in the city of Montreal, adultery was committed. The names of the respondent and corespondent are given.
Evidence was given by the petitioner before the committee of the other place in substantiation of these allegations and by two witnesses, who were investigators, namely Mr. Etheridge and Mr. Paquette, to the effect that adultery was committed. According to page 9 of the evidence the petitioner appeared, was sworn and asked certain questions by the clerk of the committee concerning her name, age, occupation and where she lived. Then the next question asked of her is:
Q. Are you married, and if so to whom?
A. I am married to-
Then, she gives the name of the husband who is the respondent in this particular case.
Q. When were you married?
A. I was married on March 8, 1928.
Q. Where?
A. Montreal.
Q. By whom?
A. By the Rev. Mr. Clare.
Q. What is your religion?
A. I am a Protestant, Unitarian.
Q. And your husband, what religion is he?
A. My husband is a Unitarian also.
Q. I show you a document. Do you recognize this document?
A. Yes, it is my marriage certificate.
Q. Are the statements therein contained true and correct?
A. They are true and correct, yes.

This would indicate that the first requirement of the bill has been met, that is that the marriage did take place and it was between the petitioner and the respondent. There is proof of the consummation of the marriage also in the fact that there were three children born of this marriage. To the extent we are permitted by the rules to make reference to these children, I would read from the evidence on page 10. Mr. Usher, who is of the city of Montreal and who was counsel for the petitioner, asks certain questions which are as follows:
Q. Are there any children issue of the marriage?
A. There are three children.
Q. Would you state the names and ages, please?
The names of the children are given and the ages also, the ages being 31, 27 and 11. Then following that there is some reference to the fact the eldest child is married and the second child is living and employed in California. The youngest child, age 11, is living with the petitioner and has lived with her and remained in her custody ever since birth.
There are extensive questions here with respect to separation proceedings. There is a question asked by Mr. Usher which appears on page 10:
Q. Is it not a fact that we instituted separation proceedings for you before the superior court in Montreal shortly thereafter?
He means shortly after a quarrel between the witness and her husband in 1957. She answered, yes.
Q. And has he ever returned to the home-
Then, Senator Roebuck says:
Is that mentioned in the petition?
Mr. Usher replies:
No, sir, the petition was taken out prior to the introduction of the legal proceedings.
There is some reference to support, which relates to the separation proceedings. The witness is asked:
Q. Was he supporting you at the time?
A. He was supporting me partially. I had to work because there was not really enough money to live on.
Q. And after he left was he sending you any support?
A. He only paid the rent because he was, of course, obliged to.
Q. And is it not a fact that by judgment of the superior court you were awarded the custody of the child,-?
A. Yes.
Q. And an alimentary allowance of $75 a month for the maintenance of your child?
A. That is right.
There is some doubt, I might say here before proceeding into the evidence, whether or not this alimentary allowance was for the
Private Bills-Divorce
child or for the wife. Some reference to that will come along in a moment. The next question is:
Q. Has he been paying the $75?
A. Sometimes, and sometimes not; very frequently not.
Q. And is it not a fact that you have had to contact our office on numerous occasions to jog your husband's memory to pay this amount of $75?
A. Yes.
Then, Senator Roebuck makes some additional inquiries. He says:
Before we leave this, Mr. Usher, I should like to ask a few more questions.
Q. You got a judgment against your husband from the court ordering him to pay you something and I think you said it was $75 a month for the support of the child?
A. Yes.
Q. And was there anything for your support?
A. None at all,
Q. Did you ask for it?
A. No.
Then, Mr. Usher assisted the committee, not by asking questions but by offering information with respect to certain legal procedures and functions of the superior court relating to the separation proceedings and allowances. He explained this to Senator Roebuck. I made reference to this before, but there is additional comment by Mr. Usher on page 12 with respect to the payment of the allowance.
I think it would be well for the committee to have an understanding, if it does not have it already, of this particular circumstance which exists in the province of Quebec. I do not know whether it exists in other provinces. In any event, it was new to me when I read the evidence and found that it existed. I think it would be somewhat enlightening to other members of this committee, if not for particular use in this instance then for use later on when similar questions arise. Mr. Usher, starting first at page 12, gave some additional information in answer to a query by another hon. senator. He said this:
Senator, probably I would be better able to answer that question. Under our jurisprudence, once there is a divorce the obligation to support the wife ceases-
This is what I was saying earlier, as you will recall, Mr. Chairman, with respect to the case with which we have just dealt. The quotation continues:
*-but the obligation to support the child remains. If there is a judgment rendered by the superior court of Montreal awarding alimony in favour of children a divorce in Ottawa does not affect that, because it is not an alimentary payment to the wife. Mr. Justice Mackinnon, I think it was, in around the year 1952 or 1953 rendered a judgment to that effect, that a divorce does not affect the alimony payable for children.
So presumably the child, who is now 11, will be financially provided for to the degree or to the extent of $75 a month regardless of

Private Bills-Divorce
whether or not this particular petition for divorce passes this place. I would assume that the lad will be fairly well looked after because additional evidence given by the petitioner, upon questioning by hon. Senator Roebuck, was as follows:
Q. The lad is going to school, is he?
A. Yes, he is going to-
And she gives the name of the particular school. The questioning continues:
Q. Are there any difficulties at home? You are out working. How old is he, did you say?
A. He is eleven.
Q. Is there any trouble in regard to taking care of him?
A. No, his school is a private school, and they are permitted to stay for sports and other different activities until 4.30. We live fairly close to the school, and he walks home, and I am home at about five o'clock. I also have the principal of the school living with me.
I would point out that subsequent questioning indicates that the principal of the school is a lady also, so there is no problem there. Mr. Usher, counsel for the petitioner, indicates he is honourary legal adviser to this particular school and that Mr. Frosst of the Frosst Chemical Company is the chairman. Everyone seems to think that the school itself is an excellent one and that the child will get a very good opportunity for education there and that the payment of $75 per month will assist somewhat in providing for and maintaining the child.
There were some events leading up to their actual separation or their actual splitting up, as it were, which, according to the evidence, took place in November of 1957 and following that, as I say, these divorce proceedings were instituted as well as separation proceedings. Mr. Usher, again with regard to the events leading up to this separation, asked the following questions:
Q. Prior to his leaving in November, 1957-
That is the respondent.
-were there any indications of immorality on his part at that time?
A. Yes, there were. I was quite certain that he was taking out some other woman at the time.
Q. What led you to that conclusion?
A. Well, I found lipstick on his clothing, and later I had a servant to take care of my child as I was working, and she said she would have to leave because of his unwelcome attentions.
That same thing occurred with the second servant in 1956. I do not relate this in order to make reference to any immoral conduct on the part of the respondent at all but for two other reasons. One is to point out that this led to some strained relationships in the family. Also, the reference to the servants being employed in the house and the reference just prior to this to the amount of rent that is being paid, notably $160 a month, which is rather a large amount to pay for

rent for an apartment, would indicate that the family was fairly well off. I do not know for a fact whether or not this is so. I only mention the amount of rent being paid and the fact that the husband and wife were working-the husband being an artist and selling antiques and so on on an independent basis-as indicating perhaps that the welfare of the child will be-at least I hope so-properly cared for if this divorce reaches the stage of being passed.
There is evidence also that no connivance or condonation took place with respect to the adultery alleged or charged. Hon. Senator Roebuck asked some questions with respect to that matter as follows:
Q. That is, you have had no sex relations with him?
That is since November, 1957:
A. No.
Q. You are complaining of some acts of adultery. Did you ever encourage them?
A. No.
Q. Did you ever connive to bring them about?
A. No.
Q. Did you throw anybody in his way for the purpose of evidence in these proceedings?
A. No.
Then he asks about matters to which I referred earlier, about the child going to school and so on. So far as collusion is concerned, there is no evidence of it but I should say there is evidence to the contrary. However, there are some strange things again when it comes to proof of adultery. I must make rather extensive reference in this instance to the evidence that is here. It is lengthy evidence. It is lengthy as compared with evidence that we have read with respect to other cases. In order to prevent myself from being accused, as I have been on other occasions, of selecting evidence to show a particular case, I shall be obliged to give the full extent of it.
Mr. Ernest Gordon Etheridge, is well known to this committee-he is an old timer -handles some 50 or 60 divorce cases a year. I think it is 60 that he is investigating or has investigated for this particular session. He has quite a wealth of experience, I am sure not only in the field of how to present evidence, not only in the field of what evidence to obtain before it is presented to the committee, not only to have a complete and thorough understanding of the specific points which he will have to prove before the committee but I am sure he is well experienced also in the field of making arrangements for particular divorces in order to ensure that a couple is seen or caught, as the expression is, in compromising circumstances which could be grounds for proving adultery. In any event, Mr. Etheridge gave evidence, as found at page 13. To dispense

with the preliminaries-that is to say, about when he was engaged and so on-and to get into the picture, he starts with the results of their investigation. Mr. Usher asks him this question:
Will you tell the result of your investigation?
A. As a result of our investigation, on the evening of Monday, May 25, 1959, I took up observation with Mr. Paquette.
Mr. Paquette is the co-investigator in this case, I suppose.
From Crescent Street we could see Mr.-
Giving the name of the respondent's green Ford station wagon, the licence number, 1959 Quebec markers. The respondent's studio and his living quarters were all in the one civic number, and he gives the number of the street in Montreal. He goes on:
During the investigation Mr.-
Giving the respondent's name.
-would use the front entrance one time out of ten possibly.
So you can see they took up rather a long vigil at this particular place if they could determine that he used the front entrance one time out of ten. I assume they had watched him on ten different occasions when the respondent had come in or gone out. He goes on:
When he would arrive and park his car in a private parking place off the laneway between-
Giving the streets.
-he would leave the car there and would go up the fire escape to his living quarters on the top of the building. They would never go around the building to go in by the front. On this evening we were there at 4.30 and about five minutes after eight we saw him leave to come down the fire escape with this woman we had seen him with on many previous occasions.
I do not know what type of fire escape it is, not having seen it, but it plays rather an important role in this evidence before us because it is the way Mr. Etheridge and Mr. Paquette, I assume it is, came to find the evidence they did. He goes on:
They parked the car on Mountain south of St. Catherine and had supper at Dinty Moore's and then they drove off as if looking for somebody in St. Lambert, where they spoke to a policeman as if trying to find an address. They finally turned around, came under the Wellington tunnel, up Mountain street and reparked the car in this parking section behind-
Then he gives an address at Sherbrooke street west. I have not given the address of this particular place where adultery is alleged to have taken place as yet, but I would point out that there is an error here in the number of the address; I think it is an error. In one reference the parking lot in the area where they lived is given-and I will only use the number-as 1330. However, 79951-0-206
Private Bills-Divorce
when they came back again and made reference to the parking section the reference was to 1130. I assume that that is a typographical error or slip of the tongue on the part of Mr. Etheridge; in any event it is of inconsequential value to this particular case here. So they came back to this particular parking section and went up by the fire escape. Mr. Etheridge continues:
After a while we noticed everything was in darkness, about 11.15. We waited shortly until before midnight and we went upstairs by the fire escape, Mr. Paquette and myself, and when we got to the door at the top of the fire escape we knocked on the door.
The house had' been in darkness for some 40 to 45 minutes, according to the evidence. They went up the fire escape, which I am sure we will all agree is not the usual means of access to a person's residence, and knocked on the door. He goes on:
Mr.-
Giving the name of the respondent.
-came and looked out-
There is no hesitation. In some cases you will notice that they knocked quite a few times after the lights had gone out for some three quarters of an hour or half an hour before somebody came to the door. But in this case the plan worked perfectly. They knocked and he came to the door just as if this was the cue after they had come up the fire escape at midnight and knocked on the door. The respondent looked out and they identified themselves to him. They stepped into the apartment after they had identified themselves. Here, Mr. Chairman, is a strange situation, as you can imagine. It is midnight, the lights had been out since 11.15, and presumably you are in bed. I am not talking about you yourself, Mr. Chairman, but through you I am speaking to the committee. You are in bed and someone comes up the fire escape, which is a strange method of getting to where you live. They knock on the door. Two strangers identify themselves to you and they step into your apartment. Then you admit who you are. In this case the respondent admitted he was so-and-so, giving his name. He also admitted that the picture in their possession was of himself. The evidence goes on:
He had come to open the door wearing the lower part of pyjamas only and he had on slippers.
Then Senator Roebuck asks:
He was nude from the waist up?
A. Yes. The living quarters consisted of a small kitchenette plus a sort of double room. It was divided with columns which separated the living room and the dining room. In the north section which was to our right with the head of the bed facing Sherbrooke street, this woman who had given us her name as-

Private Bills-Divorce
Giving the name of the corespondent.
-was lying in the open studio couch on the side closest to the wall. We could see from where Mr. Lamartine had risen from his side of the pulled-out studio couch to come to answer the door.
Q. What was she wearing?
A. She was covered to the neck with a sheet. It was a warm night and there were no spreads or blankets on the bed-
And so on. Here again we are asked to accept point blank this sort of evidence. Two strangers come up a fire escape at midnight and knock on a door which is immediately opened. They walk in, identify themselves, show a picture to someone they do not know and who does not know them. He says, "Yes, that is I". He identifies the picture. Then they ask a woman who is in bed covered up to the neck with a sheet what her name is, and she without qualms or questioning says that her name is so-and-so. From the evidence we have read in other cases threats have been used, as they were in the last instance where the investigator said they had ways of making it tough for her if she did not tell them her name. We have had instances where the investigator has rifled through women's purses, in effect committing trespass, and in that case we might expect it. But in this particular case-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Just one or two comments about this particular case, Mr. Chairman. In this particular case the lawyer, Mr. Usher, has done a service, I think, to the committee in his remarks regarding the connection between the House of Commons and a divorce granted in a legislative manner and those people in Quebec who were fortunate enough prior to their application to parliament to apply to the superior court of Quebec for relief for the female spouse and maintenance of the children. I think it is worth while to read what Mr. Usher said. He is asked:
Q. If you get this divorce is he bound to continue paying that $75?
Then Mr. Usher said:
Senator, probably I would be better able to answer that question. Under our jurisprudence, once there is a divorce the obligation to support the wife ceases, but the obligation to support the child remains. If there is a judgment rendered by the superior court of Montreal awarding alimony in favour of children a divorce in Ottawa does not affect that, because it is not an alimentary payment to the wife. Mr. Justice Mackinnon, I think it was, in around the year 1952 or 1953 rendered a judgment to that effect, that a divorce does not affect the alimony payable for children.
I am very pleased that Mr. Usher, a very competent lawyer, put this on the record, because I think it is advice that should be taken by those who are applying. In this case, as reported later on, it is evident

that there are three children of this marriage. One of them is grown up and married, the other has a good job and is living away from home, and the third is a young boy who is attending a private school. The father is now paying $75 for his maintenance, and because this has been taken through the civil court in Quebec he will continue to receive the $75 for his education.
I think it would be a pleasure to meet Mr. Usher because I was interested in the remarks he made in this case. The committee will remember that he did ask a question about the husband's conduct and the chairman, Senator Roebuck, had to point out to him that he was not to put answers into the mouth of the witness. I think this is a common court procedure, and we do not hold that against Mr. Usher though we commend the chairman of the committee for his vigilance and for asking that the question be reworded and that it should ask for an answer rather than indicate an answer. It is amusing to read what occurs as reported on page 13 when the committee was discussing the school the boy was attending.

I might say that this is an usually good school. It is probably the leading school in Montreal. That is the private progressive school of which Mr. Frosst of the Frosst Chemical Company is the chairman, and I happen to be honorary legal adviser to the school.
There is nothing like tooting your own horn. He was certainly doing that. He was giving full credit to the firm he represents, to the school, and to himself, as well as to Frosst chemicals, and I would say he did very well as far as the handling of this case is concerned with regard to the welfare of the young lad who is still dependent on the support he is receiving from his father.
I was interested in reading this case to note that once again we have the same kind of stereotyped evidence as has continually been given in the cases we have examined so far. The investigator in this case is a particularly well-versed man, Mr. Etheridge, who has the record in the Senate for presenting these cases. His record is high, and he is one of the top two or three detectives, but again we are asked to give credit to evidence the nature of which stretches our credulity. In this particular case they talk about taking up observation with Mr. Paquette. That particular answer continues:
From Crescent street we could see Mr. Lamartine's green Ford station wagon ... parked there. Mr. Lamartine's studio and his living quarters were all in the one civic number.
I notice that a great deal of questioning was done in relation to the studio and to the work of the respondent in this case. It is mentioned that he is an artist of one kind

or another. Senator Roebuck himself asked a question about his occupation when the committee was discussing whether the money was being paid for the support of the child. On page 11 the following appears:
By Senator Lambert:
Q. Is he an independent artist, or is he associated with a commercial art firm?
A. He is an artist, and he also has been selling antiques.
Q. But he is not attached to a lithographing firm or any commercial art firm?
A. No.
By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. He just sells pictures?
A. Yes, portraits, and he designs.
Senator Lambert: He is an independent artist.
On reading this I am forced to come to the conclusion that some discussion of this case must have taken place prior to the examination, and to the evidence which was given according to the transcript, because why are all these questions asked about what type of an artist this person is, where he worked, whether he worked for a lithographic firm or a commercial art firm, and so on? I suppose the temperament of people who are artists in the true sense of the word must vary. An artist with one kind of temperament may paint landscapes; an artist who paints portraits may have a different type of temperament and, again, a further type of temperament may be found in an artist who works for lithographic processes.
Nevertheless, I fail to see why all these questions were asked about the type of art work which was done, unless they were intended to establish the personality and mental attitude of the respondent. When Senator Lambert ends up, he says: He is an independent artist. In fact, he was answering a question which had been asked earlier by Senator Roebuck, which gives me the impression that more investigation was conducted into this phase of the personality of the respondent in this case than appears in the evidence, and I am curious as to whether this was done before the hearing; whether Senator Lambert may have had some knowledge of this particular person or if it was one of those affairs which sometimes happen and in this case I presume the Senate committee sat around a few minutes before the session opened and discussed a number of things and exchanged some information. Sometimes members come to an arrangement about how far they are going in questioning and what would be acceptable as a cut-off as far as questions are concerned. In court cases, quite often, they decide what they will settle for. In murder cases the lawyers and the judge may sit down and agree they will settle for second degree manslaughter.

Has the hon. member one jot or tittle of evidence to back up such a 79951-0-2061

serious statement? I know he would not wish to be unfair in this matter. Is there any evidence to support that allegation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a most unwarranted reflection on the other place.

No. It is the questioning itself. It is odd questioning, and I will just read what was said earlier with reference to alimony. The committee discussed first of ail the proceedings in the Quebec court. The record continues:
Q. Is it not a fact that we instituted separation proceedings for you before the superior court in Montreal shortly thereafter?
A. Yes.
Q. And has he ever returned to the home-

No, sir, the petition was taken out prior to the introduction of the legal proceedings.
Q. Has your husband ever returned to your home since then?

A. He was supporting me partially. I had to work because there was not really enough money to live on.

By the Chairman (Senator Roebuck):
Q. How far is he behind?
A. At the present moment he is one month behind.
Then they launched into a discussion of what kind of artist he is and they drew conclusions. I am not interested in this field but I do not think there is much connection between a lithographing firm, a commercial art firm, the selling of antiques and the work of artists as we know it. I may be drawing an inference that is not there but I am-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not even intelligent.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -led to believe that there must have been some discussion beforehand about the kind of artist he was because the questions bear no relationship to those asked previously.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, is the hon. member suggesting that the Senate has cooked up the evidence in this divorce case? Is he suggesting that there

was some impropriety on the part of the Senate in handling this case? If so, I think he should be compelled to state the grounds on which he bases his accusation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is shocking.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If the hon. member had followed what I was saying he would know there seems to be some questioning that does not have any beginning. How would you know?

Q. What led you to that conclusion?
A. Well, I found lipstick on his clothing, and later I had a servant to take care of my child as I was working, and she said she would have to leave because of his unwelcome attentions.
Q. That was shortly prior to-.
A. That was in 1955. There was then a second girl, a second servant, in 1956 who had the same difficulty with him.
Before the end of this session it is to be hoped that we will have some of these investigating officers come up before us so we can inquire into their capabilities and the methods they use. The evidence here, as in some other cases, is, to say the least, surprising. Mr. Etheridge testified as follows:
During the investigation Mr. Lamartine would use the front entrance one time out of ten possibly. When he would arrive and park his car in a private parking place off the laneway between Crescent and Mountain street, he would leave the car there and would go up the fire escape to his living quarters on the top of the building. They would never go around the building to go in by the front.
From reading the evidence I have not been able to establish if he could get in by any other means. As the apartment was laid out this would be the door normally used. I continue:
On this evening we were there at 4.30 and about five minutes after eight we saw him leave to come down the fire escape with this woman we had seen him with on many previous occasions. They parked the car on Mountain street off St. Catherine and had supper at Dinty Moore's and then they drove off as if looking for somebody in St. Lambert, where they spoke to a policeman as if trying to find an address.

I suggest they should have had the policeman stop the car behind them and find out why they were being followed around the city, but they did not. I continue:
They finally turned around, came under the Wellington tunnel up Mountain street and reparked the car in this parking section behind 1130 Sherbrooke street west and went up by the fire escape. After a while we noticed everything was in darkness, about 11.15. We waited shortly until before midnight and we went upstairs by the fire escape, Mr. Paquette and myself, and when we got to the door at the top of fire escape we knocked on the door. Mr. Lamartine came and looked out and we identified ourselves to him and we stepped into the apartment after we identified ourselves, and he admitted he was Mr. Gert Lamartine and also the picture in our possession was of himself. He had come to open the door wearing the lower part of pyjamas only and he had on slippers.
Is this normal procedure, Mr. Chairman? If somebody raps on the door at twelve o'clock at night is it not normal to ask who is there? I doubt whether there are many people, even in those areas where it is normal to leave the door unlocked, who would get up in the middle of the night, open the door and welcome in somebody whom they had not seen before. Even if he identified himself, the identification he would have to use would be a detective's badge, a driver's licence or something of that nature. I would be surprised if they do not use some form of intimidation, because with their detective's badge, or whatever they are issued in the city of Montreal or in the province of Quebec for this purpose, unless they use some type of intimidation I would be surprised if they would be readily allowed in the apartment. I go on with the evidence as to what they saw in the room.
Q. He was nude from the waist up?
A. Yes. The living quarters consisted of a small kitchenette plus a sort of double room. It was divided with columns which separated the living room and the dining room. In the north section which was to our right with the head of the bed facing Sherbrooke street, this woman who had given us her name as Nanette Lalonde was lying in the open studio couch on the side closest to the wall.
When did she give them her name as Nanette Lalonde? From my reading of the evidence I do not find that they had contact with her previously. This was the first time they had spoken to this woman-it would appear that way anyway-and yet he said:
-this woman who had given us her name as Nanette Lalonde was lying in the open studio couch on the side closest to the wall.
This is not very good evidence. They knew the name of the girl and they say that she had given her name to them previously. If we assume that-we will give the benefit of the doubt to the investigators-they may have used the wrong tense or something of that nature yet it would seem that they were
Private Bills-Divorce
familiar with the name of this young lady before they entered the room. This might indicate that she was either well known as a woman of the street which would not form the basis of an adultery charge in this case, as people of that nature are taken care of by civil law, or that the evidence in this particular is not correct.
Will the hon. member permit two questions? First, is there any evidence to suggest that she was a woman of the street? Second, has the hon. member read the evidence at the bottom of page 14?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
To answer the first question, I am not suggesting that. If I were suggesting that I would quote authorities to indicate that a divorce could not be granted if that were the case. I am not suggesting that.
To answer the second question, I have read the evidence on page 14 but the Senate committee had not heard the evidence given on page 14 when they were taking the evidence which appears on page 12. It would appear to me that you have to follow some pattern. What this witness is suggesting is that they knew her previously. We may even find it to be true that his partner had made inquiries. But in reading the evidence up to this point there is no indication that they had previously met her. I continue with the answer:
We could see from where Mr. Lamartine had risen from his side of the pulled-out studio couch to come to answer the door.
This is only an assumption; it is not a fact. It is an assumption that they could see from where he had risen to come to answer the door. They could not very well see that unless they had their eyes to the keyhole. They should have said that if they had. I would think that would be much better evidence than some of the evidence they have given. I continue:
Q. What was she wearing?
A. She was covered to the neck with a sheet. It was a warm night and there were no spreads or blankets on the bed, just the sheet.
By Mr. Usher:
Q. Was there any clothing about the place?
A. The woman's clothing was on a chair in the left-hand corner but we did not see any of Mr. Lamartine's clothing around at all.
Maybe he arrived from across the hall, or some place, in that kind of attire. If there were no clothes lying around and he went to the door wearing the lower part of his pyjamas probably he wandered in out of the hall or from some other place. I continue:
A. The woman's clothing was on a chair in the left-hand corner but we did not see any of Mr. Lamartine's clothing around at all.
Q. How many beds were in the room?
A. It was not a bed, it was a studio couch used as a bed.
Q. The woman you saw in the bed, was she Mrs. Lamartine who is sitting here?

Private Bills-Divorce
A. No, I am seeing Mrs. Lamartine for the first time.
Q. But she is not the woman you saw in the bed that night?
A. Definitely not.
This is the kind of evidence we continually get. Why did they not ask where his clothes were? These people are willing to search purses and steal nameplates oil doors, and do a number of other things. They threaten people and yet they did not look around to find out whether his clothing was there. Why did they not ascertain that? Why did they not see whether there was another door leading into that room because it would appear from the evidence that the only way you can get into that apartment is by way of the fire escape. It was a very small apartment. It would seem that is the door they used, the one that leads in off the back entrance. I continue with the evidence. Mr. Paquette, who has appeared on a number of occasions, was also questioned as to the events that evening.
Q. Were you in the company of the previous witness, Mr. Etheridge, on the night of May 25, 1959?
A. Yes sir.
Q. Would you look at this photograph already filed as exhibit 2 and state who that is?
A. I know this man as Mr. Gert Lamartine.
Q. Will you tell the committee what occurred on that evening when you obtained access to the premises of the respondent, Mr. Gert Lamartine?
A. We went up to his living quarters by the rear entrance that night, it was 11.50 p.m., to the same door as they went in previously during the evening. Mr. Etheridge knocked at the door and it took a minute or two before Mr. Lamartine came to the door. So we identified ourselves and we went into the kitchen. And after that we went into this room which is the living quarters, and in that apartment there was an open studio couch where we noticed a woman about 35 years old was lying in bed. Mr. Etheridge showed him the picture that he had in his possession and he admitted that was his picture, and he asked the woman in the bed what her name was and she said it was Nanette Lalonde.
It is surprising, Mr. Chairman, that this answer should have come from the assistant because he says that Mr. Etheridge showed him the picture that he had in his possession and he admitted that it was his picture, and he asked the woman in the bed what her name was and she said it was Nanette Lalonde. On the previous page of the testimony, the testimony of Mr. Gordon Etheridge, he said that she had previously given her name. Let me quote it:
-this woman who had given us her name as Nanette Lalonde.
In other words, Mr. Etheridge is indicating he had been previously introduced to this lady and now his partner is saying that Mr. Etheridge asked her what her name was and she had told him.
Q. What was she wearing?

A. She was covered up to the neck with the sheet.
Q. Did you see any of her clothes in the room?
A. Her clothes were on a chair beside the bed.
Q. What was Mr. Lamartine wearing?
A. The lower part of his pyjamas. We told Mr. Lamartine that Mrs. Lamartine was taking divorce action against him. Then, we took a sketch of the place and went out.
This is the type of evidence which, I would suggest, leads to only one conclusion and that is that this divorce evidence was framed. The whole thing worked out very well because the particulars had been agreed upon and the access to the apartment was of the easiest sort. In this connection I should like to ask the sponsor of this bill if he will accompany me to the Lord Elgin or Chateau Laurier, and at 12 o'clock we will rap on all the doors along one hall to ascertain how many rooms there are to which we gain access. Let us see how many people even ask us who we are or what we want. I am quite sure we will have the private detective from the hotel follow us and throw us out before we even get to the second door. I have been thrown out of better hotels than they have in Ottawa on various occasions, anyway.
Will the hon. member permit me to decline the invitation? I do not mind being thrown out of high class hotels, but not under those circumstances.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This is in the interests of research. I am sure that if we rapped upon the doors of 10 rooms we could not get into more than one. We would probably find that there was only one person in the room. We will not find one situation of this type. If there are any of these situations in the better class hotels in Ottawa tonight we would not be allowed in those rooms. I am quite willing to try it. In every case we have handled lately there is a rap on the door at one o'clock in the morning, the door opens and somebody is invited in. They must be very hospitable in Montreal. I hope to go down to Montreal this week, and I hope that what I read here is true because I am going to see for myself. This comes under the heading of research. If it is this easy to make friends and carry on a conversation with people at one o'clock in the morning, when they are engaged in something that is a criminal offence-well, it seems to me that this just does not happen. I am quite sure it does not happen.
I believe that we have here another case in which the evidence has been prepared. I have no particular objection to this divorce being granted, but I have every objection to the members of this committee being used in this particular way. I have satisfied myself from reading the evidence that the only

child who is under age is being taken care of properly and I think the wife can take care of herself. It has been pointed out that the respondent is not a very good artist. He does not work steadily and he has had trouble paying the $75.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

Clause agreed to.
Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

The house in committee on Bill No. SD-40, for the relief of Larry Orsa-Mr. McCleave- Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I had better make sure that I return the notes from the last case so I will be relating my notes to the evidence that is before us and not to some other petition. I do not know that it would make much difference, in any event, because most of these cases are of a stereotyped nature, as has been ably demonstrated by the hon. member for Timiskaming, and as has been shown in practically every bill with which we have dealt up to this time. The evidence is obtained in a certain, set pattern, and the case before us is no exception except that the investigators in this instance really got their wires crossed when it came to giving evidence of what they had seen at the particular place where the adultery was alleged to have been committed.
In this instance the couple were married on February 14, 1953 and the adultery is alleged to have taken place on June 20, 1959. These allegations are shown in the petition, and proof of the marriage is given when the petitioner is shown a document which he identifies as his marriage certificate. In this instance we will not run contrary to the ruling of the Chair and the rules of the committee in so far as the discussion of children is concerned because there are no children as a result of this particular marriage. I assume that since that is the case we will have to come to our own conclusions as to whether or not the marriage was consummated. There is some comment in the evidence about that.
Some strange things did take place. I should like, if I may, to make reference to some of them by reading the evidence and relating portions of the evidence to other portions of the evidence concerning the circumstances and relationships between the husband and wife. The petitioner is being
Private Bills-Divorce
questioned by Mr. Usher, who is counsel in this instance for the petitioner, and they talked about the husband and wife living together. This continued from the time of the marriage until April, 1957 and then Mr. Usher says:
Q. What happened then?
A. Well, we were quite happily married until the year 1957, but previous to the day she left me life was quite different at home so I did not have the affection I used to have before. She used to come in quite late at night and I tried my best to help her and to see what was going on. She was carrying on night after night coming home later from work. She used to work for her father to which I objected and she said I am just helping my father, but I realized that was not right because she was coming late at nights and giving me all kinds of excuses and I tried to find out where she was going and she was not going to the movies where she said she was and therefore I asked her what was the matter. Then in April one day she said "I am going to tell you frankly I don't love you any more, I don't want to be with you, I want to leave you". 1 said, "Well, after all, it has been four years we spent together and now you want to leave me". She said, "1 am sorry, I don't love you any more, I don't want you any more". I said, "Listen, let us do something to help ourselves, I was good to you, what is the matter?" And she said, "I am sorry but that is it". The next day when I came back from work the lady took all her belongings and she left home.
This is only part of it, but here there is an indication that the petitioner, prior to the wife leaving home, was concerned and wanted to effect a reconciliation. There is evidence about it later on, too. Another question is asked:
Q. Did you later find out where she went to?
A. Yes, I phoned her father at his residence and asked him where she was.
So apparently her father had told him where she was because he answered the query by saying yes.
Q. Did you later find out where she went to?
A. Yes, I phoned her father at his residence and asked him where she was.
Q. Did she ever come back to the home since then?
A. No, sir, I asked her several times to come back but she did not want to.
Q. What eventually developed?
There is more reference to these attempts to effect a reconciliation.
A. Well, I had been calling her up several times to come back and to help me in the house, and all she said was that she did not want to talk to me, that that was the finish. I called her several times more in 1958-
You will notice the use of the words "several times" in both years, I assume in 1957 and in 1958.
-and asked her if she wanted something in the way of help but she said, "I am quite happy and I am working and I don't want anything from you."
Later on the chairman, Senator Roebuck, made some inquiry about this self-same subject matter as follows:
Q. You had a number of conversations with her. Did she ever tell you what she was doing?

Private Bills-Divorce
A. No. She said she loved somebody else and she did not want to be with me any more. I asked her who is it.
Q. Did she tell you who it was?
A. No, she would not tell me.
Q. Or where she was living or what she was doing?
A. No, she would never tell me, she said, "Don't bother me and don't call me any more."
Then they make reference to collusion with which I will deal later on but at this stage I want to confine my remarks to this bit of evidence here. You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that the petitioner says that on a number of occasions-several times in 1957 and several times in 1958-he phoned her or called her, that he phoned her father and from her father found out where she had gone. We assume that he found out where she was living or where she was working or something of that nature. As I said, he called her several times wanting to effect some reconciliation, wanting to see whether the difficulties could be smoothed over. But then when he is asked by Senator Roebuck whether he knew where she was living he Says, "No, she would never tell me where she was living or what she was doing". It seems a bit odd that a person who is this much concerned-and I am not suggesting there is anything untoward in his evidence or in the manner of the presentation of it- who phoned her father and discovered where she was living, and had phoned her several times over a period of two years, should turn around and say that he does not know where she was living or what she was doing, -and that is what his evidence is here-that she would not tell him. If a person is that much interested in and that desirous of effecting a reconciliation of a disrupted marriage such as this man has been, and phones her several times and knows where her father is, it seems strange that he was either unable or unwilling, whatever the case .may be, to take the next obvious step and find out where she was living or where she was working. However that may be, this is the evidence that is contained here.
I should now like to turn to the evidence about adultery. Mr. Gerard Daigneault and Mr. Jerry Brault are co-investigators in this particular case. They worked together and discovered that certain things existed. Starting at the bottom of page 11 Mr. Daigneault was asked some questions by Mr. Usher, counsel for the petitioner:
Q. I understand you were engaged to investigate the conduct of the respondent in this case,-?
And the name of the respondent is given.
A. Yes.
Q. Will you look at this picture filed as exhibit 2 and state if you recognize the person shown in it?
A. That is Mrs.-.

And he gives the name of the respondent. Q. Will you tell the committee the result of your investigation?
A. Our services being retained by you during the middle of May, 1959, at which time you furnished us with that photograph here and also gave us some particulars, and 1 found Mrs.-
And he gives the name of the respondent. -to be living at-
And he gives the particular address.
-with a man.
Then the chairman, Senator Roebuck-a dear friend with whom I have had some conversation in the newspapers and probably will have some more-says this:
Wait a minute. That is a conclusion that you are drawing.
Then the senator asks this question:
Q. You found her living at-.
And that particular address is given. The question continues:
Tell us what you saw and heard.
A. As a result of this investigation, on June 20, 1959, at approximately 11.30 p.m., accompanied by Mr. Brault, we both proceeded to-
And this particular address and apartment number are given.
-where after knocking on the door a few times-
I notice that he is a little bit more up to date than are some of the other people. He has to knock a few times in order to get an answer.
-the door was opened by a man and at that time he was wearing blue pants and the top of his underwear and black shoes.
This colour combination had some relevancy-the blue pants and the black shoes- with which I will deal later on.
I identified myself to him and asked to speak to Mrs.-.
And the name of the respondent is given. The witness continues:
This fellow could not understand English very well and I asked him what nationality he was afterwards and he told me, Greek. So finally by asking him and showing him the picture we understood each other. So I walked into the apartment and there on an open studio couch used as a bed was Mrs.-
And the name of the respondent is given.
-lying on the righthand side of the bed. I asked her if she was Mrs.-
And he gives her married name.
-and she said yes, she was, and I showed her the photograph and she identified the photograph as of herself.
Then Senator Roebuck asked this question: Q. She identified it as hers?
A. Yes, as her photograph. I told her she would be hearing, and I told this to the man too, from the real husband's attorney in the near future. I asked the man for his name and he answered-

And he gave them a name, the name ol the corespondent.
Q. Did he spell it for you?
A. That is the way he gave it to me.
I therefore assume he did not spell it. Then Mr. Usher asked the condition of the respondent.
Q. What condition was she in, what clothing was she wearing?
A. When I spoke to her in the bed and she sat up she had on the upper part of blue and white pajamas.
If you will allow me to transgress for just a moment, I should like to ascertain whether this is what Mr. Brault discovered also, that she was wearing blue and white pajamas. From a quick look it does not seem as though he noticed what she was wearing. In any event, there was only one bed in the room. It was a one-room apartment. It was a studio affair that opens out into a bed. This was at 11.30 in the evening and there were only a few clothes that they noticed. Then Mr. Jerry Brault was called as a witness and sworn and was asked these questions by Mr. Usher:
Q. Mr. Brault, were you in the company of the previous witness, Mr. Daigneault, on the night of June 20, 1959?
A. Yes.
Q. Would you look at this photograph which has already been filed as exhibit No. 2 and state who that is?
A. That is Mr.-
Then he gives the name of the petitioner. There must be something wrong here unless they got the photographs mixed up in this case also. I suggest that when you get up in your eighties it is possible for this to happen. Exhibit 2 is supposed to be a picture of the wife, yet Mr. Brault identifies it as a picture of the husband or the petitioner. This is not the only error or confusion which exists in his mind as to what occurred on that evening. He is asked:
Would you state what happened that evening?
A. I accompanied Mr. Daigneault-on June 20, 1959 on a Saturday night. Mr. Daigneault knocked at the door and a man came and opened the door wearing grey pants and the top of his underwear and brown shoes.
Here we have Mr. Brault, one of the investigators identifying the picture as somebody that it is not. We are not seeing too clearly. We have him giving us identification of clothing worn by the respondent, namely that he is wearing grey pants and brown shoes, when Mr. Daigneault, the other investigator, says he was wearing blue pants and black shoes. There is a mix-up as to what was actually worn by the individual. Then he goes on:
Mr. Daigneault Identified himself and asked to talk to him inside, so we walked in the room. Mr. Daigneault told the man that we wanted to see the
Private Bills-Divorce
woman who was in bed on the open couch. So Mr. Daigneault went beside the bed and asked the woman her name, and she admitted she was Mrs. -and admitted the picture in our possession was her picture.
I would assume it is a typographical error when he identifies the picture earlier as that of the petitioner, when it is in fact the picture of the wife. I do not think we can attribute to any typographical error the difference betweeen blue and grey and black and brown when it comes to identifying the clothing worn by the person who came to the door. Both these gentlemen, Mr. Daigneault and Mr. Brault, appeared as investigators and witnesses in a number of other cases, and in all probability they will appear as witnesses and investigators in a number of other cases as time goes on. They should certainly know if they are paying attention to what they are doing that they should develop their perceptibility and notice things they desire to notice about which they know they will have to give evidence if and when they appear before the Senate committee. Unless they have become so used to these particular cases being given just cursory examination in their passage through this house and the other place, and unless by habit they have fallen into error of being sloppy in their obtaining evidence-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I let my hon. friend go unchallenged when he made a very snide remark about the chairman of the committee of the other place, but I do not think it is justice that a gentleman in that house should put up with that sort of language. It is a definite breach of the rules of the house, because as the hon. member knows one must not reflect upon the conduct of people in the other place who are not, above all, here to defend themselves. Two very serious remarks have been made. One was a very snide reference to a person over the age of 80 and then a remark about sloppiness, and I hope my hon. friend will have the grace to withdraw both those statements.
If I could speak to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that I made no reference to the chairman of the committee of the other place.
You did.

My hon. friend says I did. He has had his opportunity to raise his point of order and speak to it. He knows the rules are such that he can speak again to the point of order. So will he let me finish what I am saying and we will go on from there, if he wants to go further, and get into more difficulty than we are already. I made no reference to that. I made reference to these

Private Bills-Divorce particular investigators being sloppy in the manner in which they obtained and presented their evidence, because as my hon. friend from Halifax knows, and as every hon. member of this committee knows, this is the first time that an extensive examination has been made by members of this house of evidence of this nature.
I would think that if more careful examination were given by members of this house in committee of the whole or in the house itself to these bills when they came before it this situation would not have developed and investigators would be more on their toes when they appeared before the Senate committee to give evidence. There are cases where investigators-I am not prepared to mention their names at the moment but I have positive proof of this-have either made damned fools of themselves or perjured themselves. And proof is there by way of conflict of evidence.
That is what I meant when I said that investigators are becoming sloppy, and I think an extensive examination of the evidence in case after case will be an indication that if parliament is going to continue hearing these cases-and I say it should not; I think there should be some other method whereby these difficulties are resolved-they should insist on the investigators being a little more careful in the manner in which they obtain and present their evidence to the house.

Mr. Chairman, may I speak again to the point of order, which I thought we were on. Rule No. 35 of the standing orders of the House of Commons provides:
No member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty... nor use offensive words against either House, or against any member thereof-
The hon. member, in my submission, has offended twice against that rule and has not withdrawn gracefully or otherwise either of his remarks which he directed particularly against the chairman of the Senate divorce committee. We all heard him make reference to that gentleman a few moments ago and the record of Hansard will bear out that his remarks about sloppiness were not directed, as he said, to the detectives but to another house. In both instances I submit he is offending against rule 35.

If I may make a comment, Mr. Chairman, I made reference to people over eighty, that is quite true. I would point out that this particular case was heard by the number one subcommittee on divorce. Present were the Hon. Senators Roebuck, chairman, Farquhar, Golding and Lambert. The ages of these gentlemen, which I have taken from the parliamentary guide, are as follows. Hon. Senator Roebuck is 82; Hon.


Senator Farquhar is 85; Hon. Senator Golding is 80; Hon. Senator Lambert is 75. So my reference to "over eighty" could apply to three of them. I made no specific reference to the chairman of the committee.
Second, if I could develop this point of order which has been raised, I say again and again that the manner in which the House of Commons has dealt with divorce petitions in the past, as every hon. member of this house knows, is to pass them en bloc 50 or 100 at a time without giving any consideration to them. It is true that we have a miscellaneous private bills committee and it is true that that committee considers the evidence before each case. How carefully they consider it I know not, but I would imagine-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You never attend.
I am not a member of the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And no other C.C.F.'er is.

Thanks for the invitation. I will ask our whip to contact yours and I will become a member of the committee. I have never yet had an invitation to be a member. Oh yes, the hon. member may be used to rushing in where he is not invited, but I like to be invited. I thank the hon. member for the invitation and if the house is pleased tomorrow afternoon to pass a motion accordingly I would be pleased to sit on the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: All you have to do is to ask your own leader.
We do not work in the same way as you-"what the leader decides". We are individuals in a democratic party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Why did you not get on the
committee?

The more questions the hon. member asks, the more he indicates he knows little about the subject matter. There are only a certain number of members established for each committee and on that number depends how many members each party may have on that committee. We have two members on that committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext: You cannot persuade one of them to give you his place?
I will try, because I have been invited to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think I should deal with the point of order which was raised by the hon. member for Halifax. The rule is clear that hon. members may not use offensive language against either house or members

thereof. I do not say that a reference to the age of members of the other place is necessarily offensive, but there is certainly an implication, and I would say that the words used by the hon. member were not beyond criticism and I would ask him to avoid any reference to the other place. The evidence may be discussed, but I do not think the manner in which it is collected should be discussed.

Very well, Mr. Chairman. I still think the evidence given by these persons indicates an extreme amount of sloppiness on the part of the investigators. I trust this observation will not offend the delicate ear of the hon. member for Halifax or yourself, Mr. Chairman. I admit that in the past I have myself been negligent in considering bills of this particular type. I have been negligent in my duty as a member of parliament. The first session I was here I became a member of the miscellaneous private bills committee, and when I discovered that the committee spent almost its whole time dealing with divorce I said: I will not have any part of that, because I do not think it is a proper function of a member to do so. Later on, I began to wonder. I thought: maybe I have been derelict in my duty in not dealing with these cases. I think most hon. members of this house have been derelict in their duty in not paying attention to the evidence before them on this subject. We are passing laws dissolving marriages and we should give them extensive study. A ridiculous situation arises if we do not give extensive study to these cases-
Order.

Suppose we do not give extensive study to this particular case, and the bill is passed. It becomes law, and the marriage is dissolved. What would happen if one year from now, for the sake of argument, one of the parties were to come along and say: this divorce was obtained by perjury? Do hon. members think parliament would then turn around and repeal the bill which was passed dissolving the marriage? What a silly situation we would face then. The marriage would have been dissolved, and if the parties concerned got married in the meantime then, legally, they would be married to two husbands or wives. That is why it is so necessary for this committee to give extensive consideration to these cases, and it is in stressing this point that I say once again that the two investigators in this particular case were very sloppy in their presentation of evidence, especially when one says the man involved was wearing blue pants and the other says he was wearing grey pants and brown shoes-

They carried on a conversation in English, I presume. The evidence states, in a series of questions and answers by Senator Roebuck:
Q. You did not speak to this man at all about whether or not he was living with this woman as man and wile?

I submit that that is the conclusion they came to; it is not substantiated by the evidence, and this evidence in the nature of things follows the pattern we have seen established in almost every case which has come before us in the last month or so. The transcript states:
So I walked into the apartment and there on an open studio couch used as a bed was Mrs. Orsa lying on the righthand side of the bed. I asked her if she was Mrs. Larry Orsa and she said yes, she was, and I showed her the photograph and she identified the photograph as of herself.

subtopic: SPEECH BY RIGHT HON. JOHN G. DIEFENBAKER, P.C., Q.C., M.P., PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA AT A STATE LUNCHEON IN HONOUR OF PRESIDENT DE GAULLE, AT THE CHATEAU LAURIER, APRIL 19, 1960-REPLY BY GENERAL DE GAULLE, OTTAWA, APRIL 19, 1960

SPEECH BY RIGHT HON. JOHN G. DIEFENBAKER, P.C., Q.C., M.P., PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA AT A STATE LUNCHEON IN HONOUR OF PRESIDENT DE GAULLE, AT THE CHATEAU LAURIER, APRIL 19, 1960-REPLY BY GENERAL DE GAULLE, OTTAWA, APRIL 19, 1960
speechtext:
Mr. President, Madame de Gaulle, distinguished guests, my first words must be to welcome you here as we gather to do honour to the President of France and I want to say to you at once, sir, within the hours that have passed since your arrival here, you must have felt the degree of Canada's regard and affection for you as the great leader of one of Canada's mother countries.
And most of what I say will be in the English language because I seem to recall that Sir Winston Churchill on a recent occasion when you conferred upon him the Cross of Lorraine stated that while in the days of war he did speak in French but the days of war were over and therefore he would only speak in English for the benefit of those that were listening to him. However, I do want to welcome you in a few words in the other official language.
(Translation)
Fifteen years ago the Canadian people welcomed the President of the provisional government of the French republic. Earlier in the war we had acclaimed the president of the French committee of national liberation. Today we welcome the President of the French republic and community. Now as before, however, it is to General de Gaulle that we offer our respect and admiration. We are happy to welcome you, as well as Madame de Gaulle who represents, in our eyes, the women of France with all their fine qualities of the heart and mind.
During those fifteen years France has recovered her elan; under your direction, France is a vital, dynamic and prosperous country which again holds the position she deserves among the great nations.
(Text)
Mr. President, when you visited London earlier this month Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth, who is our Queen, said to you that Britain and France were joined to Canada and the United States by ties of history, culture and language.
May I illustrate how truly and unforgettably Her Majesty's words applied to Canada.
Only a few acres from where you sit now, Mr. President, walked the sons of France,
who more than three centuries ago began this nation's days-explorers like Samuel de Champlain, to whose memory stands a monument on a nearby cliff and missionaries like the immortal Jean de Brebeuf, who on his way to martyrdom camped for three days only a few miles from this spot; and those equally heroic souls, Father Gabriel Galena ent and Father Jogues.
These were the men, Mr. President-and there were many others-who brought to this land and carried to its farthest frontiers the eternal verities of civilization-the men who in regions of darkness and terror and awful solitude endured for France and their faith-the men of whom the historian Park-man wrote:
Men steeped in antique learning, pale with the close breath of the cloister, here spent the noon and evening of their lives, ruled savage hordes with a mild parental sway and stood serene before the direct shapes of death.
These were the men-the sons of France, of our first Canadian story-their treasurable contribution in our memories forever.
We remember, and will remember forever, that dread hour in 1940 when you, a lonely and desperate figure of destiny, clari-oned the world for France and for freedom- that clarion call which, as Her Majesty said truly to you in London, matched the winged words of Sir Winston Churchill.
And we remember, too, sir, how in the long dark days which followed, those days when liberty was under siege, those days which tried through and through every quality and mystery of the human spirit, you stood as France incarnate, the valiant trustee of her ancient glory.
There is our remembrance that in the soil of France tens of thousands of our sons rest in the quiet of God's acre-our sons who, in two world wars, went out from us into the night for freedom. In many hundreds of plots throughout the hills and valleys of France lie our dead, in resting places dedicated forever to their memory and cared for tenderly by the people of France.
Those are our memories. Those are the thoughts that come to us on this day. You have truly brought a new strength to France at home and abroad. By your compatriots

you have been entrusted with the responsibility of restoring the stability of the French state; through the courageous application of your powers, France is firmly embarked on a brilliant renaissance. You have opened the door to an honourable settlement in Algeria; and, in territories where the tricolor has flown for generations, you have been the builder of the community of independent states joined by a common loyalty to the traditions and ideals of democracy.
This visit is an important one in that it has provided an opportunity for a continuation of the discussions between us which began in Paris in November 1958. The intervening months have been fateful for our civilization. We are approaching a stage of decision, a time when the quality of leadership will be submitted to its sternest test. Personal contacts on the highest level have been multiplying since our last meeting and have been an essential preliminary to the formal meeting of chiefs of state and heads of government which you will attend in Paris a month hence. Although not a participant at the summit, Canada has none the less a vital concern with the outcome. We will be following with intense interest the discussions that take place and the decisions that are made.
Today in our discussions we have examined together the outlook for peace. You have learned something of the elements of our thinking on the great issues of foreign policy. None of them is greater than an end to the arms race with its financial burdens on national economies and all its grave dangers that armaments mean to peace. France and Canada are partners in the search for a disarmament agreement as members of the ten nations committee now meeting in Geneva. Our objective, as is your objective, is peace. I express the hope that if out of the summit comes a new understanding as between west and east and a realization that the insane waste of armaments must end, we may yet see the day when east and west may join together, join together in a major step forward, first in reducing armaments and secondly in raising the standards of men everywhere in a world offensive against poverty.
I can't express to you, sir, what this meeting has meant to my colleagues and myself, as you honoured us today by meeting with us in our cabinet. We will always have those disagreements, even the best families do, misunderstandings take place but above everything else, the leaders of the free world dare not forget that the consistent and continuing consultation at a high level is necessary at all times to assure the most effective cooperation and that unity which has been
so apparent during your visit here and meant so much to me, when you honoured Canada in November 1958, when my wife and I were with you in Paris.
Canada honours you as the wartime soul of France and a realistic and idealistic statesman of his country's restored strength and power.
For these reasons, Mr. President, because of what you are, what you have been, and what you represent, and because you come to us as a tried ally and friend, on behalf of the Canadian people I salute you with admiration, and for them say to you with the heart of all Canadians, "Vive la France".
Mr. President, you have our full attention. (Translation)
General de Gaulle: Mr. Prime Minister, the words which you have addressed to me have moved me deeply. In thanking you on behalf of France, I want to tell you of my own impression on coming in contact with Canada.
The first voice I hear in Canada is that of history. France will always pride herself in having brought to your soil, more than four centuries ago, the germs of civilizing progress and the breadth of the Christian spirit. If, later on, other developments and influences made their mark here; if there were rivalries, battles and dismemberments, nevertheless the seed sown by France in Canada grew strong, even though other harvests have also ripened. Briefly, just as one sees water plants rise to the surface, so I feel, rising from the depths of the past, all sorts of ties, attractions and similarities which draw the spirit and the heart of my country very close to those of yours.
This was made abundantly clear during the two world wars. How could we, Frenchmen, ever forget the talents displayed and the prodigious sacrifices of so very many of your soldiers during the first world war on the battlefields of Artois and Flanders, and the heroic ranks of those buried in the soil of France? How could we fail to bear in mind your exemplary participation, during the second world war, in the great battles of Normandy, of Picardy, of Belgium and Germany, which meant the liberation of Europe? How could I fail to keep alive the memories of the two visits I have previously made to Canada, one in 1944 when I saw you straining in your war effort; the other in 1945 on the morrow of victory; while you were already beginning to recover, and you were holding out the hand of help to a ravaged France? I cannot fail, in this regard, to hail the memory of Mackenzie King who led his country, while I was leading mine, through those glorious trials.

And now, how do you appear to us? Materially, a new country, of vast size, mighty resources, inhabited by a hard-working and enterprising people. Politically, a state which has found the means to unite two societies, very different in origin, language and religion; which exercises independence under the British crown and forms part of the commonwealth, which is forging a national character even though spread out over three thousand miles alongside a very powerful federation; a solid and stable state, as proven by the fact that, in the last twenty five years, only three Prime Ministers-my friends, Mackenzie King, Saint-Laurent and Diefen-baker-have headed its government; a state which, far from concentrating only on its internal problems, makes its voice heard and plays an active part in the great affairs of the world. Finally, on the moral plane, Canada appears to us as a people very sensitive on the one hand to an orderly society, and on the other hand to the liberty and dignity of men.
Therefore, be well assured that the country, the entity, the people that you are, arouse the highest interest, sympathy and confidence of France. Not only have Canada and France no dispute over claims or ambitions, no difference of fundamentals, but, on the contrary, the French feel in common accord with Canadians, both in their conception and handling of the problems of our times.
Moreover, France, a country with a thousand years behind her, is also a new country, a country finding herself again, reshaping herself, but whose stability and reviving strength underline still further her worldwide responsibilities, illuminate her idealthat of desiring for others the same selfdetermination that she wishes for herself, and which fortifies her resolve to form a vital part of what we, the free peoples, represent.
But what is our objective? In truth, it is peace, even though we realize that, to achieve it, we will have to travel a long and difficult road. In this regard, my country welcomes the approaching meeting of the heads of state commonly referred to as "the big four". France believes that there should first be introduced among these four states-and hence between the two camps of which they are the leading spirits-a relaxing of tensions. This implies the avoidance, at present, of any debating stalemate, and especially of any threat regarding, for instance, the problems of the German people. The matter also calls for at least a beginning to nuclear disarmament, starting with missiles and aircraft that carry atomic weapons, and over which mutual control is still practicable. Finally, there must be organized a basis of co-operation that will transcend political rivalries in the development of needy peoples.
At all events, France believes that the future of peace-and on this hinges survival-depends essentially upon the whole of Europe and upon America, which cradled modern civilization and are its fountainheads. France believes that the existence of opposing systems-assuming that the course of events does not narrow the gap between them-should not prevent peaceful co-existence, failing which nothing could, in the long run, save mankind. France hopes that, in going to the summit, she will enjoy the direct support of vigorous Canada, so worthy and able, and which she holds so close to her heart.

Tuesday, April 26, 1960
